opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it came from a pretty simple place. When I was finishing my PhD, I looked at myself and asked: do I actually have a research vision of my own yet? Not just a few papers, not just a technique that worked, but a set of questions I'd want to spend the next ten years on and could convince students to spend their best years on with me. And my honest answer was no, not yet.

A faculty position isn't just a promotion from being a student. You're responsible for people. A PhD student is betting five or six years of their life on your judgment. If I didn't have a clear sense of what problems mattered and why, I felt it would be almost irresponsible to take that role. So "not worthy" wasn't really false modesty. It was me recognizing that I hadn't finished becoming the kind of researcher I wanted to be.

There was also the environment. Going into industry research, to a place like FAIR at that time, felt like a continuation of my education, maybe an even more intense one. You were surrounded by people who had been thinking about these problems for decades, with the resources to try ideas at scale and the freedom to fail. I learned a lot there, not just technically, but about taste: which problems are worth working on, when to push and when to let go, and how to tell real progress from something that just looks good on a benchmark.

Looking back, I think that feeling was healthy. A bit of insecurity, if you handle it right, pushes you to keep learning instead of settling into an identity too early. When I eventually decided to go into academia, it felt different. I had things I genuinely wanted to say and explore, and I felt I could offer students something real. So I don't regret waiting. I think I needed those years to earn the confidence, at least in my own eyes.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his hesitation to lacking an independent research vision and feeling unready to guide students. It does not say he felt outside the established career path toward a faculty position.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it came from a very simple place: when I finished my PhD, I looked at the people who were getting faculty positions around me and I didn't think I was at that level. That's not false modesty. I had done some work I was proud of, ResNeXt and some of the earlier things, but a lot of that felt like I was riding on the momentum of a very good environment, very good collaborators, a very good advisor. I had a hard time separating what was mine from what was the system around me.

And there's a second layer to it. A faculty job isn't just "can you do research." It's "can you define a direction, can you convince students to spend five years of their lives on it, can you raise money for it, can you stand in front of a room and say this is what matters." At that point I didn't have a direction that I believed in strongly enough to ask other people to bet on it. I had problems I found interesting, but that's different from having a thesis about where the field should go.

So I went to industry, to FAIR, and I think that was the right call for me. Industry gave me time to just do the work without having to perform conviction I didn't have yet. I got to see what scale actually does, what fails when you have resources and what still fails even when you have resources. Slowly I started forming opinions that were actually mine. And at some point the feeling flipped. It wasn't "am I worthy of a faculty position," it was "I have things I want to say and students are the people I want to say them with." That's when I felt ready to apply, and that's when I went to NYU.

Looking back, I think the feeling of not being worthy was partly accurate and partly a distortion. Accurate in the sense that I really wasn't ready to lead. Distorted in the sense that nobody is ready, and the people who looked ready to me were mostly just better at hiding the same doubt. If I could tell my younger self one thing, it would be that readiness is something you build by doing the job, not something you need before you start. But I also wouldn't trade the years in industry. They gave me the content that made the confidence real rather than performed.

r001.rationale: He says he did not think he was at the level of peers pursuing faculty jobs and was not ready to lead, but does not explain his hesitation as feeling outside an established career path toward a faculty position.

astra-6.text:
I think “not worthy” describes a feeling more than a conclusion about my ability. When I thought about becoming a professor, I imagined someone who had a clear research direction, could consistently come up with important questions, and was ready to guide students. Looking at myself at the end of my PhD, I wasn’t confident I could do all of that yet.

There’s a difference between being able to carry out a research project and feeling ready to take responsibility for an independent research agenda. You can have work that other people appreciate and still wonder how much of it came from your own judgment, how much came from your environment, and whether you could do it again.

So I would put it less harshly now: I didn’t feel ready. That uncertainty was real, but calling it a question of whether I was worthy made it much more personal than it needed to be.

r001.rationale: The response explains his hesitation as uncertainty about readiness for an independent research agenda, but does not say he felt outside the established career path to a faculty position.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it was less that I believed I could never be a professor, and more that I didn’t feel ready to become an independent researcher. During a PhD, you can do good work and still wonder how much of it comes from you and how much comes from the environment—your advisor, your collaborators, the problems you’ve been exposed to. For me, the question was: if you took that support structure away, could I still identify important problems and develop my own research direction?

At the time, I wasn’t confident enough in that. And a faculty position means more than doing research yourself; you’re also taking responsibility for students and helping them find their direction. That felt like a big commitment. So “not worthy” is probably too harsh a way to put it. It was more a feeling that I needed more time to develop my judgment and understand what kind of researcher I wanted to be.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his hesitation to doubts about being ready to work independently and take responsibility for students. It does not say he felt outside the established career path toward a faculty position.
